ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness in Columbus, OH
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection for Columbus, Ohio plants, boilers, tanks, piping and structural steel, on your site. Request a UT quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Columbus, Ohio
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic thickness testing and ultrasonic weld inspection for Columbus, Ohio owners: boiler and process piping in manufacturing plants, pressure vessels and storage tanks, structural steel on building and bridge work, and machined or fabricated components in metal shops. Technicians are mobilized to your site with calibrated gauges and flaw detectors, work to a written procedure and report against the code you name. Request a UT inspection quote for your Columbus site and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic inspection is used in Columbus

Columbus is not a refinery town, and that shapes the work. The Columbus region counts more than 1,800 manufacturing establishments across automotive, machinery, materials, electronics and aerospace, and most of them run steam, compressed air, hydraulic and process systems that eventually need a wall-thickness record. Add the hospitals, universities and office towers that dominate the urban core, a growing base of logistics buildings, and new advanced-manufacturing construction, and the demand for UT is spread across many small and mid-sized jobs rather than a few giant shutdowns.

Typical UT scopes in this market include:

  • Thickness surveys on plant steam, condensate and compressed-air headers in stamping, casting and assembly plants.
  • Shell and head readings on air receivers, deaerators and process vessels registered with the state.
  • Floor and shell readings on aboveground tanks at fuel and chemical terminals around the metro.
  • Groove-weld examination on structural steel for new industrial buildings, crane runways and bridge repairs.
  • Wall checks on hot-water and chilled-water piping in campus and hospital central plants.
  • Material checks on plate, forgings and castings arriving at fabrication shops.

What UT finds and what it misses

An ultrasonic probe sends a short sound pulse into steel and times the echo. For thickness testing the echo from the back wall gives remaining metal; for weld examination an angled probe sends shear waves through the weld volume, and reflections from flaws appear on the display between the entry point and the back wall. That makes UT the usual tool for internal conditions that no surface method can see: general corrosion and erosion loss, laminations, lack of fusion, cracks and slag inside a weld.

The limits are just as important. Rough, scaled or heavily painted surfaces scatter sound and need cleaning. Pitted walls can give a false, thicker reading with a single-element probe. Coarse-grained castings and austenitic welds attenuate the beam. A thickness gauge reports one point under the probe, so a survey is only as good as the grid it follows. We state these limits in the procedure and the report so the owner knows what a clean result does and does not prove.

Codes, standards and the Ohio regime

Thickness work follows the practice in ASTM E797 and the thickness provisions of ASME Section V, with the measurement requirements described in the Article 5 and thickness measurement guide. Weld examination is written to Section V Article 4 and judged against the construction code: ASME B31.3 for process piping, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 for vessel welds, ASME B31.1 for power piping, or AWS D1.1 Clause 8 for structural steel. Inspection programs on existing vessels and tanks often follow API 510 and API 653, where the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection and we supply the thickness and flaw data.

Ohio regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Division of Industrial Compliance in the Department of Commerce. The state's rules adopt the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and the National Board Inspection Code, and inspections of registered equipment are done by state general inspectors and by commissioned special inspectors, many of them employed by insurers. Our readings feed those inspections; they do not replace the commissioned inspector's role.

How the work is done

For thickness, the technician calibrates a gauge on a step block of the same material, using a dual-element probe where the inside surface is corroded because it handles pitting better than a single crystal. Readings are taken at the condition monitoring locations the owner has marked or at a grid we lay out, and the A-scan is checked wherever a number looks suspicious. Hot lines call for high-temperature probes, suitable couplant and a temperature correction.

For welds, the technician builds a distance-amplitude reference from side-drilled holes in a calibration block, scans the weld and heat-affected zone with 45, 60 or 70 degree angle beams from both sides where access allows, and sizes any reflector that exceeds the recording level. Indications are plotted by distance from a datum, depth and length, then compared with the acceptance table in the code that governs the job.

Surface preparation and access for UT in Columbus plants

Most poor ultrasonic data traces back to the surface under the probe. Loose scale, flaking paint, weld spatter and rust pits all leave air gaps that couplant cannot fill, and a reading taken over a gap is either missing or wrong. On a Columbus plant floor that usually means light grinding or wire brushing at each test point, done by the owner's maintenance crew before the technician arrives, or by us under an agreed scope. Coated pipe can often be read through sound coatings if the procedure has been qualified for it, but peeling coating is removed locally.

Access matters as much as surface. Overhead headers need scaffold or a lift; vessel shells need a clear working height; tanks need a safe approach to the shell and roof. Confined-space entry, hot work permits and lockout are handled under the host site's rules, and the quote lists what we expect the owner to provide so there are no surprises on the day.

Typical UT scopes and the references behind them

Common ultrasonic scopes for central Ohio owners
ComponentWhat the technician recordsTypical reference
Plant steam and condensate pipingWall thickness at elbows, tees and low pointsASTM E797, ASME B31.1
Process piping weldsVolumetric indications in groove weldsASME Section V Article 4, B31.3
Pressure vessel shells and headsCorrosion loss and weld flawsASME Section VIII, API 510
Aboveground storage tanksShell courses and floor plate thicknessAPI 653
Structural steel groove weldsLack of fusion, cracks, slagAWS D1.1, AWS D1.5
Plate and forged stockLaminations and internal discontinuitiesASME Section V Article 5

Trending thickness data over time

A single survey tells an owner where the wall is today. Repeated surveys at the same locations tell them how fast it is thinning, which is what drives inspection intervals and replacement planning. We mark each test point with a durable identifier, record the grid in the report, and use the same calibration approach on each visit so readings compare cleanly with earlier campaigns. Where an owner already keeps condition monitoring locations in a spreadsheet or database, we match their numbering and return data in the layout they use, so the new readings drop straight into the existing trend.

Corrosion rates calculated from two surveys are only as reliable as the measurement scatter, so we note probe type, gauge settings and surface condition for each point. If a location reads thicker than last time, the report flags it for review instead of quietly accepting the change.

Who performs and reviews the work

The company has no Columbus office, so the crew travels to your site for the agreed scope. Technicians are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: a Level II technician sets up equipment, performs the examination and interprets results, while an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Because the employer, not a training provider, issues the qualification, owners with their own written practice can ask us to follow it instead. Our Level III consulting and written practice development pages explain how that works.

What the UT report contains

Every report identifies the component or line number, the drawing or isometric reference, material and nominal thickness, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, and the technician's name and level. Thickness jobs include a grid or point map with each reading, the minimum found, and a flag for any location under the owner's retirement or alert thickness. Weld jobs include scan sketches with indication location, amplitude, length and depth, and a plain accept or reject against the named criteria. Raw readings come as a spreadsheet when the owner wants to trend them against earlier surveys.

Planning a UT job in Columbus

Central Ohio winters are cold but relatively dry, with a January average low near 22 degrees Fahrenheit, and summers are warm and muggy with average July highs above 85. Cold affects couplant behavior and gauge batteries on outdoor tanks and structural steel, so we choose couplant to suit the surface temperature and keep calibration blocks at the same temperature as the work. Humidity is high through much of the year, which matters for condensation on cold steel before a survey. Insulated lines need the owner to open or remove insulation at the test points ahead of time.

Many Columbus plants run continuous production, so surveys are often arranged around planned maintenance windows and line changeovers. Expect site orientation, badge or escort requirements and lockout rules; hospitals and campus plants add infection-control and noise restrictions. Rickenbacker, the Norfolk Southern intermodal terminal area and the interstate belt around the metro make access straightforward for mobilization, but warehouse construction and busy production floors mean laydown space for ladders and lifts should be agreed in advance.

Calibration and verification during a survey

A thickness gauge is only trustworthy if it is checked against a known value at the start of the survey, again whenever the probe or cable changes, and at the end. We calibrate on a step block that matches the pipe or plate material, verify the reading on a second step, and record the block, gauge and probe serial numbers in the report. If the end-of-job check drifts, the readings since the last good check are repeated rather than adjusted on paper.

UT, MT or PT for your Columbus job

Choose UT when the question is remaining wall or an internal weld flaw. For surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, magnetic particle inspection in Columbus is faster at the surface, and for stainless steel, aluminum or non-magnetic parts, liquid penetrant testing in Columbus applies. Many boiler and vessel shutdowns combine all three. The national ultrasonic testing page and the ultrasonic testing guide cover the method in more depth, and the Ohio inspection services page shows how these services fit together across the state.

Training your own UT technicians

Plants that would rather build in-house capability can look at the UT Level 1 course and the UT Level 2 course, rehearse on the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator, and check requirements in the SNT-TC-1A eligibility guide. Details for the metro are on the Columbus NDT training page; the employer still issues the final qualification under its own written practice.

faq.q: Can you do ultrasonic thickness testing on plant steam and air piping in Columbus?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your Columbus plant, survey headers, elbows and low points on a marked grid with a calibrated gauge, and give you a thickness map with the minimum reading flagged against your alert level.

faq.q: Do you inspect boilers and pressure vessels registered with the state of Ohio?
faq.a: We take thickness and weld-flaw data on boilers, receivers and vessels. The commissioned state or insurer inspector remains responsible for the statutory inspection and certificate; our data supports that inspector's decision.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic weld inspection cover that surface methods do not?
faq.a: It examines the weld volume, so it can find lack of fusion, slag, cracks and incomplete penetration inside the joint. Surface methods such as MT and PT only reveal discontinuities open to or near the surface.

faq.q: How do you handle hot piping or insulated lines?
faq.a: High-temperature probes and couplant are used for hot surfaces, and readings are corrected for temperature. Insulation must be opened at each test point by the owner or a contractor before we start.

faq.q: Can UT replace radiography on a weld?
faq.a: Only where the construction code, the owner and the engineer agree. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each have their own UT provisions, and the substitution has to be settled before the job, not after.

faq.q: What code will the UT procedure follow?
faq.a: The one your contract names: ASTM E797 and ASME Section V for thickness, and Article 4 with B31.3, Section VIII Appendix 12, B31.1 or AWS D1.1 for welds. We write the procedure to that edition and have an ASNT Level III approve it.

faq.q: Do you have a Columbus office or lab?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Columbus. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and quotes are scoped from your drawings, access notes and the code you need.

faq.q: Can you train our maintenance staff to do their own thickness readings?
faq.a: Yes. The UT Level 1 and Level 2 courses and the practical simulator prepare candidates, and your company qualifies them under its written practice based on SNT-TC-1A. The qualification itself is issued by the employer, not by Atlantis.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Columbus, OH
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (mag particle testing) for Columbus, Ohio welds, cranes, press tooling, castings and steel, on your site. Request an MPI quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Columbus, Ohio
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection on carbon and low-alloy steel for Columbus, Ohio owners: weld repairs on boilers and vessels, lifting gear and crane components, heavy tooling and press frames, castings and forgings, and structural steel on building and bridge projects. Technicians are mobilized to your site with yokes, particles, a light meter and field-strength indicators, and they report against the code you name. Request a mag particle testing quote for your Columbus site and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used around Columbus

Central Ohio makes things from steel and moves them by road and rail. Automotive and mobility plants in Marysville, Columbus and the surrounding counties stamp, weld and assemble steel bodies and chassis parts; machinery and materials makers supply them; and fabrication shops turn out structural and plate work for the building boom around the metro. All of that equipment fatigues. Press frames crack at corners, crane hooks and lugs wear, welds on conveyors and tooling distort and crack under cycling, and every one of those cracks starts at a surface where a magnetic method sees it well.

Examples of MT work in this market:

  • Press frames, die shoes and tooling bolsters in stamping plants, checked at corners and bolt-hole edges.
  • Hooks, lifting lugs, shackles, spreader beams and below-the-hook devices on overhead cranes and rigging.
  • Weld repair excavations and finished repairs on boilers, receivers and process vessels.
  • Structural connections, base-plate welds and crane-runway steel on industrial buildings and distribution centers.
  • Steel bridge members and diaphragm connections where state or county bridge work calls for weld examination.
  • Gears, shafts, spindles and rebuilt machine components returning to service.

What magnetic particle inspection finds, and what it misses

When a steel part is magnetized, a crack or seam that breaks the surface forces magnetic flux out into the air, and fine iron particles gather over the leak to draw the flaw as a visible line. The method applies only to ferromagnetic material, which covers carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic grades but excludes austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper and most nickel alloys. It finds surface and slightly subsurface discontinuities; deeper flaws and wall loss are invisible to it.

Two points control quality. A crack lying parallel to the magnetic field produces almost no indication, so the surface is examined twice with the field turned roughly ninety degrees. And particle build-up needs a clean, dry, bare surface, so heavy scale, oil and thick paint are removed first. Thin sound coatings are sometimes acceptable if the procedure has been demonstrated through them, but a coating of unknown thickness is not assumed to be harmless.

Codes and acceptance criteria that govern MT work

The method itself is written to ASME Section V Article 7, as explained in our Article 7 guide, with ASTM E1444 and the ASTM E709 guide behind it. Acceptance depends on the job: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds and AWS D1.5 for bridge welding. API 510, 570 and 653 repair work follows the construction code that applies to the equipment, and the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible for the inspection while we deliver the examination results.

In Ohio, boilers and pressure vessels fall under the Division of Industrial Compliance in the Department of Commerce, whose rules adopt the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and the National Board Inspection Code. Welded repairs and alterations on that equipment involve commissioned inspectors and authorized repair organizations, and MT of the finished weld is usually one of the records they review.

How the examination is done

For field work the standard tool is an electromagnetic yoke. An AC yoke is used for surface work and must meet the lifting-power check in Article 7; DC and permanent-magnet yokes need a stronger pull to qualify. Where a yoke cannot reach, prods or a coil may be used under the procedure. Dry powder suits rough or hot surfaces, while wet visible or fluorescent particles give higher sensitivity on cleaned parts, and fluorescent work needs a darkened area and a UV-A source measured at the surface with a calibrated meter.

The technician checks field strength with a pie gauge or shim indicator, applies the particles while the field is on, examines overlapping areas, and repeats at the second orientation. Where residual magnetism could affect welding, machining or a later process, the part is demagnetized and verified with a gauss meter before it goes back into service.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis keeps no Columbus office; examiners are mobilized from elsewhere to your site for the agreed scope. Each holds a qualification issued under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up equipment, applies the method and interprets indications, while an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews reports. If your own written practice governs the work, we can follow it, and our written practice development and Level III consulting pages describe the support available when procedures need to be created or reconciled.

What the MT report contains

A report names the component or weld number, the drawing reference, material and surface condition, the procedure and revision, the equipment and its calibration status, the technique (yoke, prods or coil; dry or wet; visible or fluorescent), field verification, the technician's name and level, and the examination date. Each indication is described by location, orientation and length, then judged against the named acceptance criteria. Photographs or sketches are included for rejectable indications, and the report states whether demagnetization was performed and verified.

Preparing parts and surfaces

Surface condition decides whether an indication forms at all. Weld spatter, loose scale, grease and lumpy paint hold particles away from a flaw or hold them where no flaw exists, so the technician requires bare, dry steel at the examination area, extending a short distance on either side of each weld. In a Columbus plant that normally means a wire brush or flap disc pass beforehand. Contrast paint is applied where white background helps dry or wet visible particles show against dark steel.

For weld repairs, the excavation is examined before rewelding and the finished repair afterward, because each is a separate record in the repair documentation. Magnetizing across a gap, a hole or a sharp change of section throws false indications, so the technician learns the part geometry before choosing a technique.

Reading and judging indications

Not every particle line is a defect. Relevant indications come from discontinuities that interrupt the surface; non-relevant ones come from magnetic writing, changes of section, or the edge of a weld; false ones come from dirt, lint or excess particles. The technician decides which is which by re-cleaning, remagnetizing, and where necessary demagnetizing and trying again at a different field direction. Only relevant indications are measured and compared with the acceptance limits.

Linear indications, rounded indications and clusters are judged differently under most codes, so the report states the shape and size, not just that something was found. That detail lets the owner's engineer decide whether to grind out, repair or accept.

Typical MT scopes and the references behind them

Common magnetic particle scopes for central Ohio owners
ComponentWhat is examinedTypical reference
Overhead crane hooks and lugsSurface cracks at load-bearing radiiASTM E1444, ASME Section V Article 7
Vessel and boiler weld repairsExcavations and finished repair weldsASME Section VIII Appendix 6, NBIC
Process piping weldsSurface and near-surface weld flawsASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3
Structural steel weldsToe cracks, underbead cracksAWS D1.1
Bridge steel connectionsFillet and groove weldsAWS D1.5
Press frames and toolingFatigue cracks at corners and holesASTM E1444 with owner procedure

Lifting equipment and fatigue-prone steel

Overhead cranes, hoists and rigging are among the most common reasons a Columbus owner calls for mag particle work. Hooks crack at the saddle and shank, lugs crack at the pinhole edge, and welded attachments on spreader beams crack at their toes. The examination is usually done as part of a periodic inspection program, with the owner's engineer or crane inspector setting the scope. We examine the load-bearing zones the program names, record each item by tag number, and report rejectable indications so the item can be removed from service before it is used again.

Fatigue shows up wherever load cycles repeat: press frames, conveyor supports, vibrating equipment skids and crane-runway welds. These areas are worth re-examining at intervals chosen from the first findings, not left to a calendar alone.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Columbus

Central Ohio is cold in January, with average lows near 22 degrees Fahrenheit and occasional dips far lower, and warm and muggy in July with highs above 85. Particle suspensions and some contrast paints behave differently at the extremes, so outdoor work on steel that has sat in the cold needs a procedure that covers the surface temperature, and very hot surfaces call for dry particles. Humidity is high for much of the year; condensation on cold steel can ruin a wet examination, so surfaces are checked and dried first.

Many Columbus plants run on tight production schedules, so mag particle work is usually fitted to planned downtime on press lines and crane inspections. Expect orientation, badging, lockout and hot-work rules at the site. Fluorescent examination needs a space that can be darkened, which on an open plant floor means a pop-up booth or a shift to a quiet period. Parts that can be brought to a booth are quicker and more sensitive than large assemblies examined where they stand, and we say so when a quote could go either way.

MT, PT or UT for your Columbus job

Magnetic particle inspection is the fast choice for surface cracks on carbon and low-alloy steel. If the part is stainless steel, aluminum or another non-magnetic material, liquid penetrant testing in Columbus is the surface method to use, and when the question is remaining wall or an internal weld flaw, ultrasonic testing in Columbus answers it. The national magnetic particle testing page, the complete MT guide and the MT versus PT comparison help with the decision, and the Ohio inspection services page lists the other services that can sit in the same scope.

Training your own MT technicians

Plants that want in-house mag particle capability can start with the MT Level 1 course and move on to the MT Level 2 course, with the NDT practice tests for exam preparation. Local details are on the Columbus NDT training page. Qualification is issued by the employer under its own written practice, which is how SNT-TC-1A works.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be done on site at a Columbus plant?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your plant or yard with portable yokes, particles and a light meter, and can examine welds, lifting gear and machinery where they stand, subject to surface condition and access.

faq.q: Which materials can MT inspect?
faq.a: Only ferromagnetic materials: carbon steel, low-alloy steel and martensitic stainless grades. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper are not magnetizable, so liquid penetrant testing is used on those instead.

faq.q: Do you check crane hooks and lifting lugs?
faq.a: Yes. Hooks, lugs, shackles and below-the-hook devices are examined at load-bearing radii and welds, with the acceptance criteria taken from the owner's procedure or the standard that governs the equipment.

faq.q: What is the difference between wet fluorescent and dry magnetic particle?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent particles under UV-A light give the highest sensitivity on cleaned parts but need a darkened area. Dry powder is more forgiving on rough or hot surfaces and works well for field weld checks.

faq.q: Why is a second examination at a different angle required?
faq.a: A crack lying parallel to the magnetic field leaks almost no flux and can be missed. Magnetizing again at roughly ninety degrees ensures cracks in any orientation interrupt the field and show up.

faq.q: Is demagnetization part of the job?
faq.a: It is performed when residual magnetism could interfere with later welding, machining, coating or service. The technician checks the residual field with a gauss meter and records the result in the report.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a Columbus office?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Columbus. Technicians are mobilized to your site, and the quote is based on your drawings, access conditions and the code the work must meet.

faq.q: Can our staff learn magnetic particle testing through Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. The MT Level 1 and Level 2 courses prepare candidates, and your company then qualifies them under its written practice based on SNT-TC-1A. The final qualification comes from the employer.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Penetrant in Columbus, OH
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection in Columbus, Ohio for stainless steel, aluminum, castings and welds, on your site. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Columbus, Ohio
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing, often called dye penetrant inspection, for Columbus, Ohio owners who need surface cracks found on materials that magnetic methods cannot handle: stainless steel piping and vessels, aluminum parts, castings, machined components and welds of every alloy. Technicians are mobilized to your site with penetrant materials, cleaners, developer and lighting, and they report against the code you name. Request a dye penetrant inspection quote for your Columbus site and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used around Columbus

The Columbus region is strong in food and consumer goods, chemicals, materials, medical and research facilities, electronics and aerospace as well as automotive. Those industries use a great deal of stainless steel, aluminum and specialty alloy, which is exactly where PT earns its place. Stainless process piping and tanks in food, beverage and chemical plants, aluminum housings and fabrications, machined aerospace-grade parts, and hospital and campus central-plant piping all need a surface method that does not depend on magnetism.

Examples of PT work in this market:

  • Stainless steel welds on process piping, tanks and heat exchangers in food, beverage and chemical plants.
  • Weld repairs on austenitic and duplex stainless steel vessels before they return to service.
  • Aluminum structures, housings and welded frames where cracking has to be checked after fabrication or repair.
  • Castings, forgings and machined parts from foundries and machine shops, checked for cracks, laps and porosity open to the surface.
  • Socket and branch welds on small-bore piping where geometry limits other methods.
  • Non-ferrous components such as brass, bronze and titanium parts in pump and valve repair.

What penetrant testing finds, and what it misses

PT detects only discontinuities that are open to the surface. A low-viscosity liquid, usually a red visible dye or a fluorescent dye, soaks into cracks, laps, seams and pores; after the surface excess is removed, a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so the flaw appears as a bright bleed-out line or dot. It works on any clean, non-porous material, ferrous or not, and it needs no electricity or special geometry.

Its weakness is that a flaw has to be open and clean. A crack smeared shut by grinding, peening or machining, or one filled with paint, oil or scale, will not take penetrant. Porous surfaces trap dye and hide indications. For that reason the cleaning step is the most important part of the job, and any mechanical working of the surface before testing is usually followed by an etch or a change in the procedure. PT will not detect internal flaws or measure remaining wall.

Codes and acceptance criteria that govern PT work

The method follows ASME Section V Article 6, explained in the Article 6 requirements guide, with ASTM E165 as the general industry practice. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 or D1.6 where structural or stainless fabrication rules apply. Repairs on equipment covered by API 510, 570 or 653 follow the construction code, and the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection while we provide the examination results.

Penetrant materials for austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys must be controlled for halogens and sulfur because residues can promote cracking in service. We check the certificate of the penetrant lot against the limits in the procedure before the work starts, which is a requirement owners with stainless or nickel assets should always expect to see in a PT procedure.

Ohio boilers and pressure vessels fall under the state's Division of Industrial Compliance, whose rules adopt the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and the National Board Inspection Code. PT of repair welds is commonly part of the documentation those inspectors review.

How the examination is done

The technician first cleans the area with solvent or detergent and lets it dry, because penetrant cannot enter a flaw that is still wet or contaminated. Penetrant is applied by brush, spray or dip and left to dwell for the time set by the procedure, based on material, flaw type and temperature. Excess penetrant is removed with solvent-dampened wipes for a solvent-removable system, or by controlled water rinse for water-washable types, taking care not to over-remove from shallow flaws.

A thin, even coat of developer is applied. After the developing time, the surface is examined under adequate white light for visible dye, or in a darkened area under UV-A light for fluorescent systems, with the light intensity checked with a calibrated meter. Indications are measured, described and compared with the acceptance criteria. The part is then cleaned of residue, which matters on stainless steel and on parts that will be welded or coated.

Temperature, humidity and lighting limits

Penetrant systems are qualified for a working range of roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit at the part surface; steel that is colder or warmer than that needs a procedure demonstrated at the actual temperature, using a comparator block or a test panel. In Columbus that is not an academic point. Outdoor tanks and structural steel can sit well below 40 in January, when average lows are in the low twenties, and sun-heated stainless in summer can climb past the upper limit, so we measure surface temperature before applying penetrant and adjust or reschedule if the surface is out of range.

High humidity affects drying time and can leave moisture in a crack mouth, and bright outdoor sunlight washes out a visible indication. Shade, a tent or work in a quieter part of the day often solves it. Fluorescent PT needs a dark enclosure, which on a busy plant floor is usually a portable booth.

Removal methods and why they matter

The three common removal approaches behave differently. Solvent-removable penetrant is wiped off with dampened cloths and suits field work on welds and localized areas, because it needs no water or drain. Water-washable penetrant is rinsed with a controlled spray, which is quicker for large or rough parts but easier to over-wash. Post-emulsified systems add a separate emulsifier step and give the highest sensitivity on production parts, but they need a proper station. For most on-site Columbus work, solvent-removable penetrant with a non-aqueous developer is the practical choice, and the procedure states the system so results can be repeated.

Who performs and reviews the work

No Atlantis office exists in Columbus, which means examiners are mobilized to your site for each scope. Qualifications are issued under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and Level II technicians apply the method and interpret the indications, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Owners who want their own procedures followed can say so at quotation, and the Level III consulting and written practice development pages cover the help available for building them.

What the PT report contains

The report identifies the component or weld, drawing reference, material and surface finish, procedure and revision, the penetrant family and lot numbers, cleaner and developer, and the pre-cleaning method. It records surface temperature, dwell and developing times, the lighting used and its measured intensity, the technician's name and level, and the examination date. Each indication is located and sized, and the result is stated as accept or reject against the code named in the order. Photographs of rejectable indications are included, and post-cleaning is recorded.

Cleaning, etching and surface preparation

Grinding, sanding, wire brushing, shot blasting and machining all smear metal across a crack mouth and can close a flaw that penetrant would otherwise enter. After any of those operations on a part that needs PT, the surface may need a mild acid or alkaline etch to open the metal, followed by a thorough rinse and drying. The procedure should state when etching is required; where it does not, a closed crack can pass unseen.

Pre-cleaning is more than a quick wipe. Oils and greases are removed with a suitable cleaner, scale and paint with mechanical or chemical methods, and the part is dried fully before penetrant goes on. On welded stainless assemblies that were pickled or passivated, residues of those chemicals are removed as well, since they can contaminate the penetrant and interfere with a clean wash.

Judging indications

A bleed-out is not automatically a defect. Rounded blobs at a weld toe may be surface porosity, a long thin line may be a crack or a seam, and an overall pink haze usually points to poor removal of excess penetrant. The technician repeats the examination where the cause is unclear, because re-application after cleaning shows whether an indication returns in the same place with the same shape.

Relevant indications are measured and compared with the acceptance rules in the governing code. Linear indications are held to tighter limits than rounded ones in most standards, so the report states orientation and length as well as location. Pictures of rejectable indications help the owner's engineer decide on grinding, repair or acceptance.

PT, MT or UT for your Columbus job

Use PT when the material is non-magnetic or the geometry defeats a yoke, and when you are looking only for cracks open to the surface. For carbon and low-alloy steel, magnetic particle inspection in Columbus is quicker and can also find slightly subsurface flaws, and for internal weld defects or corrosion loss, ultrasonic testing in Columbus is the right tool. The national penetrant testing page and the MT versus PT comparison explain the differences, and the Ohio inspection services page shows how the three methods fit into a shared scope.

faq.q: What materials can liquid penetrant testing inspect?
faq.a: Any clean, non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium, brass and carbon steel. It finds only discontinuities open to the surface, so it is limited to surface cracks, laps and pores.

faq.q: When should I choose PT instead of magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Choose PT when the part is non-magnetic, such as austenitic stainless steel or aluminum, or when geometry stops a yoke from magnetizing the area. On carbon steel, MT is often faster.

faq.q: Can PT be done outdoors in a Columbus winter?
faq.a: Only if the surface is within the temperature range the procedure covers. Colder steel needs a procedure demonstrated at that temperature, or the work is moved to warmer conditions, because penetrant behaves differently when cold.

faq.q: Why does cleaning matter so much?
faq.a: Penetrant cannot enter a crack filled with oil, paint, scale or water. Poor cleaning hides real flaws, and surfaces smeared by grinding or machining can close cracks, so cleaning is checked before any dwell begins.

faq.q: Do you control chlorine and sulfur on stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. Penetrant lots are checked against the halogen and sulfur limits in the procedure before use on stainless or nickel alloys, and residues are removed after the examination.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible dye is read under white light and works well in the field. Fluorescent dye is read under UV-A light in a darkened area and detects finer indications, so it is used where higher sensitivity is required.
